text.p: House Speaker Newt Gingrich survived another challenge to his leadership, but the Republican Party skirmish claimed a rising young conservative, Bill Paxon, who quit a key post on Thursday.

"I'm the speaker. We're winning," Gingrich told reporters but he declined to discuss the implications of Paxon's resignation as chairman of Republican Party's House leadership team, a post to which he was appointed by the speaker. Paxon, Republican of New York, said Gingrich no longer trusted him.

Lawmakers who have been among those upset with Gingrich's handling of the party's agenda this year, speaking on background, said the latest flap began last week when the issue of ousting Gingrich came up at a private meeting. They said the outcome left relations among the party's leaders strained.

But moderate Republican Representative Sherwood Boehlert said Gingrich had a wide base of support across the conservative and moderate wings of the party and saw the challenge as having come from a handful of members.

"Last week there was turmoil, and a week later one guy (the speaker) emerged above all the others," said Boehlert, of New York. "I think he will reassess his relationship with the leadership," he added.

Boehlert also suggested that other top Republicans, House Majority Leader Dick Armey of Texas, Republican Whip Tom DeLay of Texas and Republican Conference chairman John Boehner of Ohio, will need to do some "soul-searching." He said Gingrich's deputies should have come out sooner and stronger in support of the speaker when reports of the coup plot emerged earlier this week.

House Appropriations Committee chairman Bob Livingston of Louisiana told reporters he expected that the speaker would rely more on committee chairmen than he has in the past. And, Gingrich spokeswoman Christina Martin said there will be discussion of changes in management style.
In his resignation, the 43-year-old Paxon, of New York cited "a growing crisis of confidence" within the party and the need to "mend its wounds."

"Both my word and my relationship with the speaker have been called into question by my involvement in last week's attempt to resolve and heal a growing crisis of confidence within our party's ranks," Paxon said in a separate statement.
The action by one of Gingrich's appointed emissaries to the rank-and-file was only the latest in a series of brush-fire challenges Gingrich has had to stamp out this year.
Gingrich has been plagued by internal party problems since he narrowly won re-election as speaker in January. He was reprimanded and fined by his colleagues for ethics violations.

In a public display of unity, Gingrich on Thursday appeared before television cameras at a news conference on taxes flanked by his deputies, Armey, DeLay, Boehner and newly elected Vice Chairman Jennifer Dunn of Washington. Republicans chose Dunn on Wednesday over a more conservative lawmaker, a development seen as a victory for Gingrich.

Boehner denied he had been at the meeting. DeLay issued a statement denying that he would resign his leadership job. Armey on Wednesday called "ludicrous" allegations that he was involved in a plot to oust the speaker. "Newt belongs in the speaker's chair, now and for years to come," he said.

Just one month ago, the party held a lengthy meeting to air disagreements after 50 critics met secretly to discuss dissatisfaction with the leadership's handling of legislation and disputes with the White House. Gingrich emerged from that meeting to state that he was still in charge. At the time, the critics denied writing a letter which urged a formal challenge to Gingrich's speakership.

The announcement of Paxon's resignation took lawmakers by surprise. Party sources said it was assumed that Gingrich had asked him to step down after reports surfaced that Paxon had attended a meeting last Thursday in which a move to oust the speaker was discussed.
"People are beginning to put the pieces together and figure out where he was on the continuum of events," a Republican who declined to be named said.

Paxon was first elected to Congress in 1988. He headed the National Republican Congressional Committee and helped engineer the party's recapture of the House in the 1994 elections after 40 years in the minority. He is married to Representative Susan Molinari, Republican of New York, who will resign in August to become a CBS weekend television news anchor. She had been the sixth ranking member in Republican leadership.
